raw_response:
I farm the same 6 mu in a wheat-maize rotation, so I will use all 6 mu for winter wheat and then all 6 mu again for summer maize. At my age, I do not like making big changes unless I see a clear benefit. I usually start from what worked before, then adjust a little for cost and weather. Since I have well irrigation, I will not be stingy with water at the key stages. For wheat, I will use improved seed, put a solid base fertilizer into the land, and then topdress nitrogen once when it starts growing strongly in spring. Wheat on our side cannot rely only on the sky; if I miss water at turning green or filling, yield drops fast. For maize after wheat, I will still use hybrid seed, because the hybrids around here give better ears and more stable yield. I will put most fertilizer in at sowing and add some nitrogen later around the big bell stage. I would rather spend a bit more on fertilizer than watch the crop go pale and lose yield. On pesticides, I do not spray for nothing, but I will not wait too long if I see aphids, armyworm, rust, or leaf disease. On 6 mu, I can still manage carefully with family labor and a few machine services, so I will keep the plan steady and practical.

decision.reasoning_summary: I will keep the usual wheat-maize rotation on all 6 mu, because that is the safest way for me to protect yield and control cost. I will use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed, because I have seen those do better in nearby fields. I will put enough nitrogen first and not cut phosphorus and potassium too hard, since weak fertilizer means weak crop and lower grain. With my well, I will water wheat three times at key stages and maize two times if rain is short. I will use rotary tillage before wheat and no-tillage maize after wheat harvest to save time. I will spray about twice for each crop, depending on insects and disease pressure, because waiting too long usually costs more than one spray.
